profiles.name: Jack Edwards
profiles.excerpt: Jack Edwards was a durable West Coast radio character actor, remembered as Skip Turner throughout Adventures by Morse and heard repeatedly in Golden Radio Hour's detective and dramatic holdings.
profiles.bio_html:
Jack Edwards belongs to the large group of radio professionals whose voices were heard constantly even though comparatively little personal biography survives. His career is nevertheless well documented through the programs themselves. Most notably, Edwards played Texas adventurer Skip Turner throughout Carlton E. Morse's 52-episode syndicated Adventures by Morse, working opposite Elliott Lewis, David Ellis and Russell Thorson as Captain Bart Friday.

Morse also used Edwards in a 1945 audition intended to revive I Love a Mystery, casting him as Doc Long opposite David Ellis as Jack Packard. Edwards later became a familiar supporting actor in Hollywood network drama, moving easily between crime stories, westerns and anthology productions. He was never dependent on one signature character; his value was the dependable character work that kept weekly dramas populated with believable policemen, suspects, gunmen and ordinary citizens.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 43 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Edwards, seven Have Gun, Will Travel appearances, six The Whistler episodes, five each on Gunsmoke and Screen Directors Playhouse, and additional work on Broadway Is My Beat, The Adventures of Philip Marlowe and The Railroad Hour.

profiles.name: Vivi Janiss
profiles.excerpt: Vivi Janiss brought a stage-trained voice to some of the strongest West Coast radio drama of the 1950s, with major GRH holdings in Johnny Dollar, Gunsmoke and Philip Marlowe.
profiles.bio_html:
Vivi Janiss was born Vivian Audrey Jamison in Omaha in 1911 and grew up around professional performers. She appeared on Broadway in the 1934 Ziegfeld Follies before building a career that moved among stage, radio, film and television. Her professional surname is most consistently documented as Janiss, although surviving radio credits sometimes shorten or vary the spelling.

Radio became one of Janiss's strongest mediums. She worked in the Los Angeles dramatic pool heard on Gunsmoke, Escape, Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, The Adventures of Philip Marlowe and other prestige series where a performer might play a frightened witness one week and a hardened frontier character the next. Her television career later extended through westerns, police dramas and anthology programs, while her voice work included an early association with Disney's Daisy Duck.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Janiss, 20 Gunsmoke appearances, 13 The Adventures of Philip Marlowe episodes, seven Escape performances, five NBC University Theater broadcasts and additional work on Barrie Craig, Lux Radio Theatre and The Whistler.

profiles.name: Russell Horton
profiles.excerpt: Russell Horton became one of the defining repertory voices of the 1970s and 1980s radio-drama revival, especially through his extensive work on CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Russell Horton, born in Los Angeles in 1941, built a career across stage, screen, commercials and voice acting. His work came a generation after network radio's first golden age, but he became important to the medium when CBS restored regularly scheduled radio drama in the 1970s. Horton could sound youthful, authoritative, comic or sinister, making him especially useful in repertory productions that demanded a new character from episode to episode.

CBS Radio Mystery Theater became the center of Horton's radio career. Reference logs credit him with well over two hundred appearances across the series, sometimes handling more than one character in a production. Outside dramatic radio he became widely heard as the voice of the Trix Rabbit and in other commercial and animation work, while film audiences may recognize his brief but memorable appearance in Annie Hall.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 91 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Horton. That concentrated holding makes him one of the clearest examples in the archive of how professional radio acting continued well beyond the 1950s and how the repertory tradition survived into the medium's later revival era.

profiles.name: Jerry Hausner
profiles.excerpt: Jerry Hausner carried a vaudeville and stock-theater background into radio, where his gift for comic characterization made him a regular on major comedy series before film, television and animation broadened his career.
profiles.bio_html:
Jerry Hausner was born James Bernard Hausner in Cleveland in 1909. He worked in stock theater and vaudeville, appeared on Broadway in Queer People in 1934, and entered broadcasting at Cleveland station WJAY. Radio rewarded the compact, expressive character acting he had learned on stage, and Hausner became a working specialist rather than a performer tied to a single leading role.

He was a regular on programs including Blondie, The Jim Backus Show, The Judy Canova Show, Too Many Cooks and Young Love. His vocal range extended even to specialized effects such as infant cries. Later audiences knew him as Ricky Ricardo's agent on I Love Lucy, as a voice performer and dialogue director in animation, and from films including Stanley Kubrick's Paths of Glory.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 13 Broadway Is My Beat performances credited to Hausner, eight The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show appearances, six Screen Directors Playhouse broadcasts, five My Favorite Husband episodes and additional work on Encore Theater, Sears Radio Theater, The Railroad Hour and Escape.

profiles.name: Minerva Pious
profiles.excerpt: Minerva Pious was one of radio comedy's great dialect performers, transforming years in Fred Allen's repertory company into the enduring Allen's Alley character Mrs. Nussbaum.
profiles.bio_html:
Minerva Pious was born in Odessa in the Russian Empire and came to the United States as a small child. Before radio became her profession she worked as a stenographer and writer, studied performance, and developed an exceptional ear for dialect. That ability brought her to Fred Allen, who hired her in the early 1930s for the ensemble he called his Mighty Allen Art Players.

Pious could play a wide range of voices, but her defining creation was Pansy Nussbaum, the quick-tongued Allen's Alley resident whose accented malapropisms became one of the program's signatures. Allen later praised Pious as an extraordinary dialect performer. Her career was broader than Mrs. Nussbaum, however: she worked with Kate Smith, Jack Benny, Bob Hope and others and appeared in dramatic radio, including Norman Corwin productions and Columbia Workshop.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 78 The Fred Allen Show performances credited to Pious, three Columbia Workshop appearances, and additional work on Duffy's Tavern and The Abbott and Costello Show. The concentration of Allen broadcasts makes her signature comic partnership especially well represented in the archive.

profiles.name: Jack Petruzzi
profiles.excerpt: Jack Petruzzi was a dependable WXYZ and network radio actor whose recurring Ed Lowry on The Green Hornet connected him to one of Detroit radio's most important dramatic companies.
profiles.bio_html:
Jack Petruzzi was part of the professional acting pool surrounding Detroit station WXYZ, the source of The Lone Ranger and The Green Hornet. Personal biographical detail about him is limited, but the surviving broadcast record shows a substantial career rather than occasional appearances. On The Green Hornet, Petruzzi became the regular voice of Daily Sentinel reporter Ed Lowry, a recurring newsroom character who admired the Hornet without knowing Britt Reid's secret.

Petruzzi's WXYZ work also included repeated appearances on The Lone Ranger, and his career extended into the broader network repertory heard on detective and anthology programs. That range matters because it places him in both the tightly knit Detroit serial tradition and the later Hollywood-style guest-cast system, where the same actor could move among westerns, crime stories and contemporary drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 38 The Lone Ranger performances credited to Petruzzi, 26 The Green Hornet appearances, seven Jeff Regan, Investigator episodes, five Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances, three The Whistler appearances and additional work on Dr. Kildare, Lux Radio Theatre and Richard Diamond, Private Detective.

profiles.name: Jan Miner
profiles.excerpt: Jan Miner was a major New York radio actress whose Ann Williams on Casey, Crime Photographer became one of her signature roles long before television audiences knew her as Palmolive's Madge.
profiles.bio_html:
Jan Miner was born in Boston in 1917 and first trained in art before turning seriously to acting. She studied with teachers including Lee Strasberg and made her stage debut in 1945. Radio quickly became a major part of her career, and by the late 1940s and 1950s she was working across several New York dramatic series at once.

Miner is especially remembered as reporter Ann Williams on Casey, Crime Photographer, a role she also carried into the television version. Her radio work also included Mary Wesley on Boston Blackie, a turn as Della Street on Perry Mason, and acclaimed anthology performances on Radio City Playhouse. Decades later, her long-running Palmolive commercials as Madge the manicurist made her face familiar to an audience that may never have realized how extensive her radio career had been.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 55 Casey, Crime Photographer performances credited to Miner, six Boston Blackie appearances, four each on The Chase and X Minus One, two each on CBS Radio Workshop and The Mysterious Traveler, and additional work on Cloak and Dagger and I Love a Mystery.

profiles.name: Clayton Post
profiles.excerpt: Clayton Post was a prolific Hollywood radio repertory actor whose surviving credits span westerns, police drama, detectives and anthology work, including a memorable Jesse James for Crime Classics.
profiles.bio_html:
Clayton Post is a good example of the working radio actor whose career is easier to reconstruct from broadcast credits than from surviving personal biography. Radio logs place him repeatedly in the Hollywood dramatic companies of the late 1940s and 1950s, where producers needed versatile supporting performers who could step into a western, police procedural or private-eye story with little fanfare and make the character immediately credible.

Post was a frequent supporting player on Wild Bill Hickok and appeared across major crime and suspense programs. One of his most distinctive surviving roles came on Crime Classics in 1953, when he played Jesse James in The Death of a Picture Hanger. His broader credits include Suspense, Let George Do It and repeated appearances with the casts of Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar and The Line Up.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 19 Wild Bill Hickok performances credited to Post, 12 each on The Line Up and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, eight each on Broadway Is My Beat and Gunsmoke, five each on Escape and Fort Laramie, and four Let George Do It appearances.

profiles.name: Les Damon
profiles.excerpt: Les Damon was one of radio's busiest leading men, moving from Hummert serials to Nick Charles on The Thin Man and Michael Waring on The Falcon while maintaining a broad repertory career.
profiles.bio_html:
Les Damon was born in Providence, Rhode Island in 1908 and trained through stock theatre before spending a year as an apprentice with London's Old Vic company. Back in the United States he found steady work in Chicago radio, including the high-volume daytime productions associated with Frank and Anne Hummert. That environment trained actors to learn quickly, differentiate characters by voice alone and move from one live broadcast to another.

Damon became a radio leading man as Nick Charles on The Adventures of the Thin Man, opposite Claudia Morgan as Nora. His career paused for military service during World War II, when he served in the Army Air Forces and earned the Bronze Star, then resumed after his return. In 1950 he took over Michael Waring on The Falcon, combining the polish of a leading man with the tougher rhythm of postwar detective radio. He later reunited with Morgan for The Adventures of the Abbotts.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 52 The Falcon performances credited to Damon, eight The Adventures of the Abbotts episodes, eight X Minus One appearances, six Words at War broadcasts and additional work on Gang Busters and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar.

profiles.name: William Griffis
profiles.excerpt: William Griffis bridged radio's science-fiction era and its 1970s revival, bringing a long stage career to X Minus One, Theater Five and CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
William Griffis was born in Hollywood in 1917 and built a career that stretched across radio, Broadway, television and film. His stage work included Broadway and touring productions, while television eventually brought him recurring work in daytime drama. Radio, however, remained part of his professional life across several very different eras of the medium.

In the 1950s Griffis appeared in science-fiction and dramatic productions such as Dimension X, 2000 Plus and X Minus One. He continued into the 1960s with Theater Five, then returned prominently during the network-radio revival through CBS Radio Mystery Theater. A 1978 CBS feature specifically identified Griffis as one of the daytime television actors who regularly worked at night on the Mystery Theater, illustrating how radio continued to employ experienced stage and television performers long after its supposed golden age had ended.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 36 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Griffis, 19 Theater Five appearances, eight X Minus One episodes, three each on 2000 Plus and Crime and Peter Chambers, two each on Dimension X and Stroke of Fate, and additional work on Rocky Fortune.
